list.listitem: Give one course of antenatal corticosteroids to mothers at risk of preterm delivery (before 35 weeks' gestation) to reduce the risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and death in their infants. A
Delay elective repeat cesarian sections until 39 weeks' gestation to prevent RDS and other adverse neonatal outcomes. B
Suspect neonatal RDS in premature infants, particularly <35 weeks, with respiratory distress. C
Give intratracheal surfactant to preterm infants <30 weeks gestation who need mechanical ventilation secondary to severe RDS to decrease morbidity and mortality.A

Consider using continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) immediately after birth with subsequent selective surfactant administration if needed as an alternative to routine intubation and administration of prophylactic or early surfactant administration to decrease mortality and bronchopulmonary dysplasia.A

background.definition: Neonatal RDS is characterized by increasing hypoxia and respiratory distress in a premature infant in the first few hours of life with characteristic reticulogranular pattern on chest x-ray. Also known as hyaline membrane disease.

list.listitem: The incidence of neonatal RDS increases with increasing prematurity.

RDS incidence by estimated gestational age (EGA) is as follows: <32 weeks: 26%; 33 to 34 weeks: 15%; 35 to 36 weeks 7%; ≥37 weeks: 2%. Estimates of RDS for <32 weeks have varied between 25% and 60%, with estimates of >80% RDS in infants <29 week EGA.
RDS incidence by birthweight is as follows: 501 g to 750 g: 71%; 751 g to 1000 g: 55%; 1001 g to 1250 g: 37%; 1251 g to 1500 g: 23%.
Neonatal RDS is the leading cause of death and disability in premature infants.
Prematurity leading to surfactant deficiency.
Neonatal RDS is caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of surfactant.
Pulmonary surfactant is a mixture of phospholipids and lipoproteins secreted by pneumocytes. Surfactant decreases surface tension of alveoli.
Lack of surfactant leads to atelectasis.
Delay elective repeat cesarian sections until 39 weeks' gestation to prevent RDS and other adverse neonatal outcomes. B

One course of antenatal corticosteroids (eg, 2 doses of betamethasone 12 mg IM 1 day apart) to mothers at risk of preterm delivery (before 35 weeks' gestation) reduces the risk of RDS and death in their infants (RR: 0.69; 95% CI: 0.58-0.81). A

A meta-analysis found that antenatal steroids at ≥34 wks gestation reduces the risk of RDS (RR: 0.74; 95% CI: 0.61-0.91). Consider a single course of corticosteroids for women at risk of imminent late premature delivery (34-36 wks gestation) and women undergoing planned cesarean delivery ≥37 wks gestation.

Multiple courses of antenatal corticosteroids are controversial. Multiple courses of antenatal corticosteroids may decrease risk of RDS and mortality, but decrease weight, height, and head circumference; long-term effects are unknown. B No evidence that antenatal corticosteroids given prior to 26 weeks' gestation prevents RDS.
Observational studies have found that in histological chorioamnionitis, antenatal steroids may reduce RDS.
Preterm infants should be delivered in a hospital with a Level 3 nursery (neonatal intensive care unit). C

A meta-analysis found that among preterm infants, the use of less invasive surfactant administration was associated with the lowest likelihood of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia at 36 wks gestation compared with nasal continuous positve airway pressure alone, intubation and surfactant administration followed by extubation, noninvasive intermittent positive pressure ventilation, nebulized surfactant administration, surfactant administration via laryngeal mask airway and mechanical ventilation.

In term (≥37 weeks) babies born via elective cesarian, one study of 942 newborns found that prophylactic betamethasone (2 doses of IM betamethasone within 48 hours of delivery) decreases the risk of NICU admission for respiratory distress (RR: 0.15; 95% CI: 0.03-0.64), but does not decrease the incidence of RDS (RR: 0.32; 95% CI: 0.07-1.58), transient tachypnea of the newborn (RR: 0.52; 95% CI: 0.25-1.11), need for mechanical ventilation (RR: 4.07; 95% CI: 0.46-36.27), or length of stay in NICU (MD: −2.14 days; 95% CI: −5.58 to 1.30 days).

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (OR: 5.39), magnesium sulfate (OR: 2.76), calcium channel blockers (OR: 2.71), and beta-mimetics (OR: 2.02) delay onset of labor in women at risk for preterm delivery, but have not been shown to lower neonatal respiratory distress.
Suspect neonatal RDS in premature infants, particularly <35 weeks, with respiratory distress within the first few hours of life. C
Obtain CXR to look for characteristic "ground glass" appearance (reticulogranular pattern). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Respiratory distress caused by lack of surfactant in premature infants; CXR with ground-glass appearance
Transient tachypnea within 1-2 hours after birth; CXR with perihilar streaking
Respiratory distress caused by aspiration of meconium during delivery, particularly in postdates infants

Differential.Differential_Name: Group B streptococcal pneumonia and sepsis
Differential.Differential_Features: Mother Group B streptococcus positive (or unknown) and not pretreated with antibiotics. Improves with antibiotics. Cultures grow out Group B streptococcus
Term or postterm infant with tachypnea, but minimal retractions. Echocardiography confirms diagnosis
Murmur on exam, minimal improvement of PaO2 with 100% oxygen. Echocardiography confirms diagnosis

list.listitem: Signs and symptoms of respiratory distress on physical examination include grunting, retracting, nasal flaring, tachypnea, cyanosis.
Gestational age is a critical risk factor, particularly history of prematurity <37 weeks' gestation.
Low birthweight infants are at increased risk.
Hypoxia as measured by pulse oximetry is present.
Chest x-ray with "ground glass" appearance (reticulogranular pattern) with air bronchograms within 6 to 12 hours after birth is typical.
ABG will show PaO2 <50 mm Hg in room air, central cyanosis in room air, or need for supplemental oxygen to maintain PaO2 >50 mm Hg.

Outpatient management of post-prematurity respiratory diseaseManaging these infants often falls to primary care pediatricians and family physicians. European guidelines based on a series of systematic reviews recommend the following:
Obtain polysomnography or overnight/24 hour pulse oximetry in infants with sleep-disordered breathing such as persistent snoring, failure to thrive, or an ongoing need for supplemental oxygen at 2 years of age. Obtain swallowing studies including videofluoroscopic swallowing study if there is cough or oxygen desaturation during feeding, vocal cord paralysis, failure to wean from oxygen over time, persistent or worsening pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, or other chronic pulmonary concerns. Further evaluation may include dynamic airway imaging with CT or MRI or airway endoscopy.
A clinical rule has been validated that predicts short-term adverse respiratory outcomes in newborns older than 34 weeks.
Consider neonatal RDS in premature infants with hypoxia and/or signs of respiratory distress (grunting, flaring, retracting).
Obtain CXR to look for ground-glass appearance (reticulogranular pattern).

Early use of CPAP or NIPPV with subsequent selective surfactant administration in extremely preterm infants compared with treatment with prophylactic or early surfactant use decreases bronchopulmonary dysplasia and death. A
Give intratracheal surfactant to preterm infants <30 weeks gestation who need mechanical ventilation secondary to severe RDS to decrease morbidity and mortality.
In infants with ongoing RDS or high risk of ongoing RDS, multiple doses of intratacheal surfactant improve morbidity and mortality. A
Neither systemic nor inhaled corticosteroids prevents development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia in infants with RDS. A

Give intratracheal surfactant to preterm infants <30 weeks gestation who need mechanical ventilation secondary to severe RDS to decrease morbidity and mortality. Intratracheal surfactant decreases risk of mortality (NNT 11), bronchopulmonary dysplasia (NNT 9), pneumothorax (NNT 6), and emphysema (NNT 5).

In infants with continuing RDS (persistent oxygen need, ventilation, >50% oxygen on CPAP 6 mm water), multiple doses of intratracheal surfactant improve oxygenation and ventilation, decrease risk of pneumothorax, (RR: 0.51; 95% Cl: 0.30-0.88), and trend toward decreased mortality (RR: 0.63; 95% CI: 0.39-1.02). In infants at high risk for RDS, multiple doses of prophylactic surfactant improve oxygenation and ventilation, and decrease risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (RR: 0.2; 95% CI: 0.08-0.51) and mortality (RR: 0.56; 95% CI: 0.39-0.81).
Animal-derived surfactant and synthetic surfactant have equivalent efficacy in preventing/treating RDS and preventing death and bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

Prophylactic surfactant in babies at high risk of developing RDS does not decrease mortality or air leak compared to routine stabilization on continuous airway pressure (CPAP) and selective use of surfactant in infants with RDS.
Give surfactant to infants with RDS as soon as possible after intubation whether or not antenatal steroids were received.

In an RCT with 103 infants 28 to 35 weeks gestation, administrering surfactant via laryngeal mask airway compared with those receiving it via CPAP only reduced the likelihood of intubation and mechanical ventilation (38% vs. 64%, OR = 0.30, 95% CI: 0.13-0.70).

A trial of 450 infants born at ≤28 weeks gestational age and at 7 to 14 days of age randomized them to late surfactant and inhaled nitric oxide versus nitric oxide alone. It found that late surfactant reduced the likelihood of requiring home respiratory support (36% vs. 53%, p <0.05) with no difference in persistent pulmonary morbidity.
Less invasive surfactant administration (LISA) uses minimally invasive catheter surfactant delivery and may be better tolerated.

A small exploratory trial compared vibrating mesh nebulizer (VMN) with less invasive surfactant administration (LISA) in 49 infants with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). The researchers found that apnea of prematurity and transient decrease in oxygen saturation were both less common in the VMN group.

A systematic review identified 16 RCTs with 1944 infants comparing LISA with intubation-surfactant-extubation (INSURE) for infants < 36 weeks with RDS. They concluded compared with INSURE, LISA decreased CPAP time, the need for mechanical ventilation and mortality.

Early (≤7 days of life) and moderately early (7-14 days of life) corticosteroids facilitate extubation and reduce the risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, but cause short-term adverse effects (GI bleeding, hypertension, growth failure, hyperglycemia, hypertrophic cardiomopathy), and possibly long-term increased neurodevelopmental impairments.

A systematic review of pulmonary application of corticosteroids identified 12 RCTs and found a reduction in the risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia or death (RR 0.85, 95% CI: 0.76-0.96). The risk of patent ductus arteriosus and pneumonia were also significantly reduced.

Long-term follow-up from a randomized trial ("Hydrocortisone for BPD") of hydrocortisone vs placebo to present BPD did not impact functional impairment at school age, with three-quarters of all children having impairment.

Late corticosteroids (>7 days of life) may decrease mortality without increasing the risk of developmental delay, but current evidence is limited. Consider a short course of late corticosteroids only in infants unable to be weaned from mechanical ventilation.
Meta-analyses found that early (≤7 days of life) inhaled corticosteroids decreases the risk of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia at 36 wks postmenstural age.
High-dose dexamethasone (0.5 mg/kg/d) is not more efficacious than low-dose steroids and is not recommended to prevent/treat bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

A Cochrane review found limited evidence to support using antenatal corticosteroids before planned caesarean in term infants. One large RCT with 942 neonates was identified and found reduced likelihlood of admission to the NICU for respiratory complications (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.90) and possibly a reduced risk of RDS (95% CI 0.34, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.65).

A systematic review identified 18 cohort studies with 33,152 evaluating use of antenatal corticosteroids in twins. They found lower odds of neonatal mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.59, 95% CI 0.43-0.80, 5 studies with 20,312 neonates) and RDS (aOR 0.70, 95% CI 0.57-0.86, 7 studies with 20,628 neonates). Since these were not randomized trials and there is a strong likelihood of residual confounding, this must be considered a very low quality of evidence.
Digoxin is not effective in infants with RDS and no CHF.

Inositol supplementation in infants with RDS decreases mortality (RR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.31-0.91), Grade 3/4 intraventricular hemorrhage (RR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.31-0.90), and retinopathy of prematurity ≥stage 3 (RR: 0.09; 95% CI: 0.01-0.67).
Intramuscular vitamin A supplementation modestly reduces mortality or oxygen requirement at one month of age (RR: 0.93; 95% CI: 0.88-0.99).
An RCT of 97 very low birth weight preterm neonates found that zinc supplementation reduces mortality (RR 0.43) and morbidity (OR 0.51).

listitem.strong: Outpatient management of post-prematurity respiratory disease

list.listitem:
Managing these infants often falls to primary care pediatricians and family physicians. European guidelines based on a series of systematic reviews recommend the following:
Do not routinely prescribe bronchodilators or inhaled corticosteroid in the absence of recurrent respiratory symptoms In those with recurrent cough or wheeze, begin with a trial of a short-acting inhaled bronchodilator Discontinue diuretics following NICU discharge "in a judicious manner"

A meta-analysis of 7 trials including 3289 infants found that avoiding endotracheal mechanical ventilation decreases mortality and development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia in preterm infants <30 weeks gestational age (OR: 0.83; 95% CI: 0.71-0.96; NNT: 35).
Nasal CPAP (nCPAP) with early surfactant decreases the need for later mechanical ventilation, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and air leaks.

An RCT of 1234 extremely premature infants found no difference in death or neurodevelopmental impairment between early nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or early surfactant administration.

A prospective cohort study following 918 infants randomized to early CPAP compared to intubation/surfactant found that infants treated with early CPAP had fewer episodes of wheezing without a cold (28.9% vs. 36.5%; p <0.05), respiratory illnesses diagnosed by a doctor (47.7% vs. 55.2%; p <0.05), and physician/ED visits for breathing problems (68% vs. 72.9%; p <0.05) by 18 to 22 months corrected age.

An RCT of 1009 extremely low birth weight infants found no difference between nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) and nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) in survival to 36 weeks without bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

A systematic review of 18 trials with 1900 infants compared nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) with CPAP for the prevention of respiratory failure. Ventilator generated non-synchronized NIPPV (RR 0.64, 95% CI: 0.48-0.85) and synchronized NIPPV (RR 0.52, 95% CI: 0.34-0.81) both reduced the likelihood of respiratory failure, as did flow-driver-generated non-synchronized NIPPV (RR 0.64, 95% CI: 0.43-0.96). The overall risk reduction for all methods of NIPPV compared with CPAP was 37% (RR 0.63, 95% CI: 0.52-0.75). The estimated NNT to prevent one episode of respiratory failure was 11.

An RCT of 432 infants ≥28 wks EGA found no difference between heated, humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HHHFNC) and nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) in subsequent need to intubation, or development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia. A Cochrane review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to establish the safety or efficacy of high flow nasal cannula in preterm infants with respiratory distress.

In neonates, volume-targeted ventilation, compared to pressure-limited ventilation, reduces the combined outcome of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (RR: 0.73; 95% CI: 0.57-0.93), pneumothorax (RR: 0.46; 95% CI: 0.25-0.84), days of ventilation (median days: −2.36; 95% CI: −3.9 to −0.8), and the combined outcome of periventricular leukomalacia or grade 3 to 4 intraventricular hemorrhage (RR: 0.48; 95% CI: 0.28-0.84).
In infants with RDS, elective initial placement on high-frequency oscillatory ventilation does not decrease the incidence of chronic lung disease as compared to conventional ventilation.
Prone-positioning improves oxygenation compared to supine-positioning in intubated infants (mean difference (MD) in oxygen saturation: 1.97%; 95% CI: 1.18-2.77).

An RCT of 98 preterm infants (24-34 weeks gestational age) found that limited oxygen during initial resuscitation (initial resuscitation with room air, with fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) increased by 10% every 30 seconds as needed to maintain appropriate oxygen saturation and heartrate) versus high oxygen strategy (initial resuscitation with 100% oxygen with FiO2 decreased every 30 seconds by 10% to keep preductal SaO2 85%-94%) decreased ventilator days (3 vs. 8; p <0.05 and incidence of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (7% vs. 25%; p <0.05).
There is no advantage of nasal prong or face mask in initial respiratory support for preterm infants in reducing intubations.
Inhaled nitric oxide in infants with RDS does not decrease mortality, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, or neurodevelopmental impairment.
All newborns with RDS should be transferred to the nearest Level 3 nursery (neonatal intensive care unit).
No difference in the development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia or neurodevelopmental outcomes after 2 years in premature infants (27-32 weeks) treated with early versus late surfactant. B
Infants born at lower gestational ages are at increased risk for death and development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (requiring supplemental oxygen after 36 weeks postconception). B

Fifty-two percent of infants with extremely low gestational age (<28 weeks) who survive have bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and 25% of those <27 weeks' gestation have severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia. B
